title: Recommendations
outcome: By the end, I can filter requirements before ranking preferences and avoid overinterpreting clicks.
scenario: A fictional classroom break chooser recommends a suitable paper activity.
given: Must be quiet and take at most 12 minutes. Score 2 for puzzles and 1 for solo.
A puzzle,solo,noisy,8 min; B puzzle,group,quiet,12 min; C drawing,solo,quiet,10 min.

steps.label: Requirements
steps.detail: Reject A because it is noisy despite a preference score of 3.

steps.label: Eligible candidates
steps.detail: B and C both satisfy time and quiet requirements.

steps.label: Recommend
steps.detail: Choose B; preserve the reasons and any later feedback.

explanation: A hard requirement determines whether an option can be chosen at all. Preferences rank the eligible options. The apparent best preference match, A, is not suitable under the quiet requirement. If a learner clicks C instead, the event alone does not tell us whether they disliked B, misclicked or wanted variety.

counterfactual.change: Change the maximum time to 10 minutes.
counterfactual.prediction: Only C remains eligible and is recommended.
counterfactual.reason: B takes 12 minutes; A is still noisy.

student_task: Why does the recommendation change without changing anyone’s preferences?
teacher_answer: The requirement changes eligibility. C becomes the only eligible choice even though B would still score more preference points.
project_evidence: Separate sorter requirements, preferences and observed feedback; document why a suggestion was eligible.
limits: One click is an observed event, not proof of satisfaction or a stable personal preference.
review_note: New fictional worked case reviewed against the weekly topic and reserved independent assessment. Keep that assessment separate; this picture is supported practice.
